lesson.title: Inside the Breadboard: Rows, Columns, and the Center Gap
lesson.summary: A breadboard is a reusable prototyping surface whose rows of holes are connected internally in short strips, letting you build and rewire a circuit just by pushing component leads and wires into holes, with no soldering required.
lesson.body:
A breadboard looks at first glance like a plain grid of holes molded into a plastic block, but the layout is not random, and understanding it is the whole key to using one. Underneath the plastic, short strips of springy metal run beneath groups of holes, and any two holes that share one of these strips are electrically connected to each other, exactly as if a wire ran between them. Pushing a component lead or a jumper wire into a hole makes contact with that strip, so two components plugged into holes on the same strip are automatically wired together with no soldering at all.

The main body of the board is organized into two halves, split by a narrow trench called the center gap. On each half, the holes are arranged in short columns of typically five, and it is the columns, not the rows, that are connected together internally: five holes running vertically in a column share one metal strip, while adjacent columns are electrically isolated from each other. This is the opposite of what the words row and column might suggest at a glance, so it is worth checking with a real board in hand: the short columns of five are your internal connection groups, and moving one column over gets you a completely separate node. The center gap exists specifically to interrupt this pattern down the middle of the board, and it is sized to straddle a standard dual in line integrated circuit chip, so that the pins on one side of the chip land in one set of columns and the pins on the other side land in a separate, unconnected set, rather than being shorted together by a single continuous strip running underneath the chip's body.

Running along the top and bottom edges of the board, separate from the main grid, are the power rails, usually marked with a red line for positive supply and a blue or black line for ground. Unlike the short five hole columns in the main grid, these rail strips run in long continuous sections down most or all of the length of the board, which is exactly what you want, since a supply voltage and a ground reference typically need to reach many different points in a circuit at once.

This whole structure is what makes a breadboard the natural first tool for the kind of prototyping described in the previous chapter: pushing a resistor lead into one column and a capacitor lead into an adjacent hole in that same column wires them together instantly, and pulling them back out and moving them elsewhere is just as fast, letting you test an idea, discover it is wrong, and rearrange the circuit in seconds. The cost of that convenience is reliability at higher frequencies and higher currents, since the spring contacts and the stray capacitance between adjacent strips are not as clean or as robust as an actual soldered joint, which is exactly why the next chapter turns to soldering as the way to make a validated prototype permanent.
